title: Wait-free algorithms: bounded progress for every thread
summary: Why lock-free CAS loops can starve a thread, which primitives can build wait-free objects (consensus numbers), and how announce-and-help makes practical wait-free queues.
outcomes: Explain why a CAS retry loop is lock-free but not wait-free, with a schedule that starves one thread
Use consensus numbers to decide whether a primitive can implement an object wait-free for n threads
Trace Herlihy's universal construction and compute when a stalled thread's operation gets helped in
Walk through the Kogan-Petrank queue's phases, descriptors and three-step helping scheme
Weigh wait-free against lock-free designs, including fast-path-slow-path and memory reclamation

lessons.title: Why a lock-free CAS loop can starve one thread

blocks.md:
In the prerequisite course you built Treiber stacks and Michael-Scott queues out of compare-and-swap (CAS) retry loops. Those structures are **lock-free**: whenever threads keep taking steps, *some* thread finishes an operation in a finite number of steps. Nothing in that definition promises that *your* thread finishes.

Herlihy's 1991 paper defines the stronger property. An implementation is **wait-free** if any process can complete any operation in a finite number of its own steps, regardless of the execution speeds of the other processes. It is **bounded wait-free** if there is a fixed number $N$ such that no operation stays pending across $N$ of its caller's own steps.

blocks.caption: The classic lock-free increment: a CAS retry loop. Every failed CAS means some other thread's CAS succeeded.

blocks.prompt: Two threads call `incr()` over and over. Is there a schedule in which thread A keeps finishing increments while thread B never finishes even one, even though B keeps running?
blocks.reveal: Yes. If the scheduler always lets A do its CAS between B's read of the value and B's CAS, B's CAS fails every time, and each failure hands B a value that is already stale by the time it retries. The system makes progress (A's increments), so the loop is lock-free, but B starves. Nothing about B's code bounds how many times it retries.

blocks.title: An adversarial schedule starves thread B

scenes.caption: B loads 0, then A loads 0 and its CAS wins (counter 1). B's CAS expected 0, so it fails and refreshes old to 1.
The pattern repeats: each time, A's load and CAS slip in just before B's retry. After 10 steps the counter is 3, A finished 3 increments, B spent 4 steps and finished none.
Same 10 steps with an atomic add that the hardware executes as one step: each call finishes in exactly one of its caller's steps, so A and B each finish 5 and the counter is 10.

blocks.md: Wait-freedom is a worst-case promise against *any* scheduler, so an adversarial interleaving like this is fair game. Herlihy motivates it with ordinary events: a thread can be delayed by a page fault, a cache miss, an exhausted scheduling quantum, or being swapped out, and some processors may simply be faster than others. A wait-free operation still finishes in a bounded number of its own steps when those things happen to the other threads.

blocks.title: CAS loop under a random scheduler (simulation)

scenes.caption: Simplified model: each step a uniformly random thread acts; an attempt is a load then a CAS, and a failed CAS reloads (unlike the code above). Mean CAS attempts per increment over 400,000 increments: 1.43, 2.00, 2.77, 3.83.
Most attempts observed for a single increment in the same runs: 13, 20, 35, 51. More samples would raise these; the model has no finite worst case.
Percent of increments that needed 5 or more attempts: 1.29, 6.81, 16.96, 29.79. The tail grows with contention even though the average stays small.

blocks.md: "It almost never retries more than a few times" is not a bound. The averages above are small, but the per-operation maximum keeps growing with threads and with how long you run, and an adversarial scheduler can make it infinite. Lock-free code gives you throughput, not per-operation latency guarantees.

Is `fetch_add` wait-free, then? It depends on the target. Where the CPU has a single atomic add instruction, each call is one step of the calling thread. Rust's standard library is explicit that its atomic types are guaranteed lock-free when available but **not** guaranteed wait-free: operations like `fetch_or` may be implemented with a compare-and-swap loop. So the progress guarantee of a primitive is a property of the platform, not of the API name.

The progress ladder, weakest to strongest: **blocking** (a stalled lock holder can stop everyone), **lock-free** (some thread always completes), **wait-free** (every thread completes in finitely many of its own steps), **bounded wait-free** (every thread completes within a fixed number of its own steps).

blocks.question: A thread holds a spinlock and gets preempted for 10 ms. During that time the other 7 threads spin on the lock. Which progress class does a spinlock-protected counter belong to?
options: Wait-free, because each spin iteration is a bounded number of instructions
Lock-free, because the spinning threads are still executing steps
Blocking, because one delayed thread stops every other thread from completing
Bounded wait-free, because the preemption lasts a fixed 10 ms
blocks.explain: Lock-freedom requires that some thread completes an operation whenever threads take steps. Here 7 threads take steps and none completes, because progress depends on the preempted holder. That is the defining weakness of blocking synchronization, and the reason both lock-free and wait-free designs exist.

blocks.question: In the simulation, a CAS-loop increment at 16 threads averaged 3.83 attempts and the worst observed was 51. What can you conclude about its worst case?
options: It is at most 51 attempts
It is about 4 attempts on average, so it is wait-free in practice
No finite bound exists: some schedule makes a thread retry forever
It is bounded by 16 attempts, one per competing thread
blocks.explain: The simulation only samples schedules. The adversarial timeline shows a schedule where B fails every time, so the operation is lock-free but not wait-free. Observed maxima are a property of the sample, not of the algorithm.

lessons.title: Consensus numbers: which primitives can build wait-free objects

blocks.md:
Which hardware primitives are strong enough to build wait-free data structures at all? Herlihy answers this with **consensus**. In $n$-process consensus, each process starts with an input value and must decide on a value so that the decisions are **consistent** (no two processes decide differently), **valid** (the decided value was some process's input), and **wait-free** (each process decides after a finite number of its own steps).

The **consensus number** of an object $X$ is the largest $n$ for which $X$, together with any number of read/write registers, solves $n$-process consensus. If no largest $n$ exists, it is infinite.

blocks.tex: \text{cons}(X)=n,\ \text{cons}(Y)=m<n \;\Longrightarrow\; \text{no wait-free implementation of } X \text{ from } Y \text{ for more than } m \text{ processes}
blocks.caption: Herlihy's Theorem 1. If Y could implement X, the consensus protocol built from X would become one built from Y.

scenes.caption: Bottom level: atomic read/write registers have consensus number 1. They cannot even let two processes agree wait-free.
Level 2: test&set, swap, fetch&add, FIFO queues and stacks solve 2-process consensus but not 3-process consensus.
Atomic assignment to n registers at once reaches 2n-2. The edges mean: objects below cannot implement objects above, wait-free, for that many processes.
Top: compare&swap, fetch&cons, a queue with a peek operation, and memory-to-memory move or swap have infinite consensus number. These are the universal primitives.

blocks.md: Why do registers fail? Herlihy's proof considers a protocol state where the outcome is still open, and the very next step of either process would decide it. Case by case: if one process's decision step is a read, the other process cannot tell the read happened; if both write to different registers, the two orders lead to the same state; if both write the same register, the second write erases the evidence of the first. In each case some process cannot tell which way the decision went, a contradiction.

scenes.caption: Each process first publishes its input in a register, so the other can read it later.
Q's test&set reaches the bit first and gets back the initial value 0, so Q knows it won and decides its own input, 9.
P's test&set returns 1, so P lost. With only two processes, the winner must be Q, so P reads prefer[Q] and also decides 9.

blocks.prompt: Add a third process R with input 7. Its test&set returns 1. Whose prefer entry should R read?
blocks.reveal: R cannot know. A losing return value says only "someone else won", not who. With two processes the loser can infer the winner; with three it cannot, and Herlihy proves no cleverer protocol fixes this. That is why test&set, swap and fetch&add stop at consensus number 2.

scenes.caption: Herlihy's protocol: r starts empty. Each process runs first = CAS(r, empty, input). P2 gets there first; the CAS returns empty, so P2 decides 9.
P1's CAS fails, but a failed CAS returns the value it found. That value is the winner's input, so P1 decides 9.
The same works for any number of processes, each in exactly one CAS. Unlike test&set, the loser learns who won, which is why CAS has infinite consensus number.

blocks.md: Compare&swap is **universal**: an object with consensus number at least $n$ can implement any object wait-free for $n$ processes (next lesson). Fetch&add, swap and test&set are not, so Herlihy proves you cannot build a wait-free compare&swap out of them plus registers for three or more processes.

Two consequences are worth memorizing. First, from read/write registers alone you cannot build a wait-free queue, stack, priority queue, set or list. Second, a FIFO queue has consensus number exactly 2: with two processes, initialize it with a winner token and a loser token and let each dequeue once; with three, Herlihy shows by a separate case analysis that no queue protocol works.

The hierarchy is about deterministic wait-free algorithms. Herlihy notes that if the guarantee may be probabilistic (finite *expected* steps), the hierarchy collapses: randomized consensus from atomic registers exists. And a high consensus number says nothing about speed; it only says what is possible.

blocks.question: You need a wait-free multi-word CAS object shared by 8 threads. Your platform offers only atomic loads, stores, swap and fetch&add. What does the hierarchy tell you?
options: It is possible but slow, because fetch&add needs helping
It is impossible: those primitives have consensus number at most 2, while CAS has consensus number infinity
It is possible because 8 threads are below fetch&add's consensus number
It is possible with enough registers, since registers have unbounded capacity
blocks.explain: Anything built from objects of consensus number 2 can solve consensus for at most 2 processes. A wait-free multi-word CAS would solve consensus for 8, so Theorem 1 rules it out. You would need a stronger primitive such as CAS.

blocks.question: Why does a failed compare&swap make the consensus protocol work for any number of processes, while a lost test&set does not?
options: CAS is faster than test&set on modern hardware
A failed CAS returns the stored value, which is the winner's input; a lost test&set returns only a bit
CAS uses more memory, so it can store all inputs
test&set is not atomic
blocks.explain: The losers' problem is identifying the winner. CAS writes the winner's value into the shared word and hands it back to every loser. test&set returns 1 to every loser and carries no identity.

lessons.title: Herlihy's universal construction: announce, then help

blocks.md:
Knowing CAS-strength primitives are *possible* is not the same as knowing *how* to use them. Herlihy's universal construction turns any sequential object into a bounded wait-free one for $n$ processes, given consensus objects (which CAS provides, as you just saw).

The object is represented as a **log**: a linked list of cells, one per operation. Each cell holds a sequence number `seq` (0 while not yet in the list), the invocation `inv`, a consensus object `new` that fixes the state and result after the operation, and a consensus object `after` that fixes which cell comes next. Applying operations in log order to the initial state gives every result.

Two shared arrays drive it. `announce[P]` points to the cell process P is trying to append. `head[P]` points to the last cell P has seen. To run an operation, P allocates a cell, **announces** it, scans `head` for the newest cell, then loops until its own cell has a nonzero `seq`. In each round P looks at the newest cell $c$ it knows and checks whose announcement is due next. If that process has an unthreaded cell, P proposes *that* cell instead of its own.

blocks.caption: The round-robin rule: the cell after sequence number s gives priority to process (s mod n) + 1.

blocks.code:
def apply_op(P, inv):
    mine = Cell(seq=0, inv=inv)
    announce[P] = mine
    head[P] = max_seq(head)               # newest cell anyone has seen
    while announce[P].seq == 0:
        c = head[P]
        help = announce[(c.seq % n) + 1]
        prefer = help if help.seq == 0 else announce[P]
        d = c.after.decide(prefer)        # consensus: one winner per slot
        d.new.decide(apply(d.inv, c.new.state))
        d.seq = c.seq + 1
        head[P] = d
    return announce[P].new.result
blocks.caption: Simplified from Herlihy 1991, Figure 14 (processes numbered 1 to n; memory reclamation omitted).

blocks.title: Round-robin helping threads a stalled process's cell

scenes.caption: n = 4. Cells 1 to 5 are in the log. P4 announces its cell now, while the newest cell has seq 5, and then stalls forever. P1 to P3 keep running operations, so their announcements are always pending too.
Whoever wins slot 6 had to propose announce[(5 mod 4) + 1] = announce[2], because P2 has a pending cell. Cell 6 is P2's operation.
Slot 7 belongs to announce[(6 mod 4) + 1] = announce[3]: P3's cell.
Slot 8 goes to announce[(7 mod 4) + 1] = announce[4]. Some running process threads P4's cell for it. P4 took no step after announcing, yet its operation is in the log, 3 cells after it announced.

blocks.md: Herlihy proves that P's loop runs at most $n + 1$ times: within that many new cells, the round-robin rule must reach P's slot, and every process appending there must propose P's cell. That makes the construction **bounded wait-free**. He also notes that without the helping step the protocol would be non-blocking (lock-free) but not wait-free: a slow process could lose every consensus round forever.

blocks.prompt: Every round, each `after.decide()` call has several proposers, but only one cell wins. Why must `new` also be a consensus object instead of a plain field that each helper writes?
blocks.reveal: Several processes may thread and initialize the same cell concurrently, and the operation may be nondeterministic, so they could compute different states and results. Making `new` a consensus object forces all of them to agree on one (state, result) pair. The `seq` field (and a `before` back-pointer Herlihy uses only for memory reclamation) is computed deterministically, so plain writes are enough.

blocks.md: The template for almost every wait-free algorithm since: **announce** your operation in a per-thread slot, then **help** pending operations in an order that guarantees each announced operation gets its turn within a bounded number of steps.

Universal does not mean practical. Every cell carries a full object state, and every operation contends on the single end of one log, so operations on different parts of the object (a queue's head and tail) still conflict. Kogan and Petrank point to these two costs, state copying and no disjoint-access parallelism, as why universal constructions are hardly considered practical.

blocks.question: Same construction, n = 4. P3 announces its cell when the newest cell has seq 9, then stalls. Under constant contention from the others, what seq will P3's cell get?
options: No bound, because P3 is stalled
blocks.explain: The cell after seq 9 is due to announce[(9 mod 4) + 1] = announce[2], so seq 10 is P2's. The cell after seq 10 is due to announce[(10 mod 4) + 1] = announce[3], so P3's cell becomes seq 11, helped in by whoever wins that slot.

blocks.question: A teammate removes the `help` lookup so each process always proposes its own cell. Which property is lost?
options: Linearizability: operations might be applied twice
Wait-freedom: a slow process can lose every consensus round, though the system still progresses
Lock-freedom: the system might stop making progress
Nothing: consensus still picks one cell per slot
blocks.explain: Each consensus round still threads exactly one cell, so the system progresses and nothing is applied twice. But nothing forces a slow process's cell to win, so that process can starve. Herlihy states this directly: without helping the protocol is non-blocking but not wait-free.

lessons.title: A practical wait-free queue: phases and helping (Kogan-Petrank)

blocks.md: Kogan and Petrank (PPoPP 2011) gave the first practical wait-free queue that supports multiple concurrent enqueuers and dequeuers, using only CAS. Earlier wait-free queues either came from impractical universal constructions or allowed only one enqueuer or one dequeuer. Their starting point is the Michael-Scott queue from the prerequisite course: a singly linked list with a sentinel, plus `head` and `tail` references.

Two additions make it wait-free:

1. A `state` array with one **operation descriptor** per thread: `phase`, `pending`, `enqueue` (the type), and `node`.
2. A **phase number** chosen as `maxPhase() + 1`, the largest phase in `state` plus one, an idea borrowed from the doorway of Lamport's Bakery algorithm. A thread publishes its descriptor and then calls `help(phase)`, which walks the whole `state` array and helps every pending operation whose phase is less than or equal to its own, including its own operation.

blocks.caption: Java, abridged from Kogan and Petrank 2011, Figures 1 and 4.

blocks.md: Helping is only safe if an operation cannot be applied twice. The paper splits each operation into three atomic steps that different threads may execute, but that cannot interleave with another operation of the same type: (1) change the list so everyone sees an operation in progress, which is where it linearizes; (2) mark the owner's descriptor `pending = false`; (3) finish fixing `tail` or `head`. Enqueue reuses the Michael-Scott lazy tail: at most one dangling node can sit past `tail`. Dequeue adds a `deqTid` field to each node; writing a thread id into the sentinel's `deqTid` claims it.

blocks.title: Enqueue 400 then dequeue, step by step (paper's Figures 3 and 5)

scenes.caption: Figure 3a of the paper. The list holds sentinel 100, then 200 and 300; head points at 100, tail at 300. The state array has one descriptor per thread; threads 0 to 3 last used phases 7, 5, 5, 6.
Thread 3 calls enq(400). Its phase is maxPhase() + 1 = 8. It writes a descriptor: phase 8, pending, enqueue, node 400 (not yet linked). Then it calls help(8).
Step 1: a CAS sets 300.next from null to node 400. This is the linearization point. Tail lags, and other enqueuers that see the dangling node must help finish it first.
Step 2: help_finish_enq reads enqTid = 3 from the new node and CASes thread 3's descriptor to pending = false.
Step 3: CAS tail from 300 to 400. The enqueue is complete. Any thread could have done steps 1 to 3 for thread 3.
Figure 5a. Thread 1 calls deq() with phase maxPhase() + 1 = 9 and publishes a pending dequeue descriptor with node = null.
Stage 1: a helper CASes thread 1's descriptor so node points at the current first node, sentinel 100. This guards against a race with a helper who saw an empty queue.
Stage 2: CAS the sentinel's deqTid from -1 to 1. This logically locks the sentinel for thread 1 and is the dequeue's linearization point.
Stage 3: help_finish_deq reads deqTid = 1 and CASes thread 1's descriptor to pending = false.
Stage 4: CAS head from 100 to 200, which becomes the new sentinel. Thread 1 returns node.next.value, the value after 100: 200.

blocks.md: Now the point of all this: helping a stalled thread. Suppose thread 1 publishes an enqueue and is descheduled before touching the list. Every thread that starts a later operation picks a larger phase, and its `help()` call walks the whole array, so it must complete thread 1's operation before it can return from its own.

scenes.caption: Simplified scenario. All descriptors are idle with phases 7, 5, 5, 6. Thread 1 picks phase 8, publishes enqueue 400, and is descheduled.
Thread 3 starts enqueue 500 with phase 9, publishes it, and calls help(9), which scans entries 0 to 3.
Entry 1 is pending with phase 8, which is at most 9, so thread 3 runs help_enq(1, 9): link node 400, mark thread 1 done, swing tail.
Only then does the scan reach entry 3 and apply thread 3's own enqueue after 400.
Thread 1 wakes, runs help(8), finds its descriptor no longer pending, skips entry 3 because 9 is greater than 8, and returns. Its 400 was enqueued without its help.

blocks.md: Why the bound holds: once thread i has chosen phase p, any operation that starts later chooses a phase above p and helps every pending operation with phase at most its own before returning, so i's operation cannot be overtaken indefinitely. Each `help` call visits each of the n descriptors once and every helping loop it runs is bounded, so its cost is bounded by a function of n, not by how unlucky the scheduler is.

Two checks in `help_enq` look redundant but are not. The paper shows that replacing `while (isStillPending(tid, phase))` with `while (true)` breaks wait-freedom, and dropping the second `isStillPending` check just before the CAS on `last.next` breaks linearizability, because a thread that was suspended there could insert a node another helper already inserted.

Practical details from the paper: the base version's `maxPhase()` and `help()` scans make even uncontended operations cost O(n); the phase counter is a 64-bit integer, so wraparound is impractical; and the Java code relies on garbage collection. For C++ the authors propose hazard pointers, which are themselves wait-free, so the queue stays wait-free (lesson 5).

blocks.question: Thread 1's enqueue was linearized by a helper, but a different helper is still suspended between marking thread 1 not pending and swinging tail. Thread 1 returns immediately and starts a new operation. What does the paper say goes wrong if `enq()` skips its final `help_finish_enq()` call?
options: Nothing, because tail is only a hint
The node is enqueued twice
Further enqueues can be blocked until the suspended helper resumes, which breaks wait-freedom
Thread 1's next dequeue returns the wrong value
blocks.explain: help_finish_enq checks that the owner's descriptor still points at the dangling node. Once thread 1 has published a new descriptor that check fails, so no one fixes tail and every later enqueue waits on the suspended helper. The final call ensures tail is past your node before you return.

blocks.question: A thread on an otherwise idle 64-thread system calls `enq()` on the base Kogan-Petrank queue. Roughly how much work does it do?
options: Constant work, like the Michael-Scott queue
Work proportional to 64, because maxPhase() and help() each scan the whole state array
Unbounded work, since helping can repeat forever
Work proportional to the queue length
blocks.explain: Even with no contention the base version reads every descriptor twice: once to compute the phase and once in help(). The paper's optimizations replace maxPhase() with an atomic counter and make help() check one or a few entries per call in cyclic order, which keeps the bound but cuts the uncontended cost.

lessons.title: Making wait-free fast: fast path, slow path, and when to bother

blocks.md: Wait-freedom costs throughput. Kogan and Petrank measured their queue against the Michael-Scott queue in Java on 8-core Xeon machines. It was typically slower: on one system the optimized wait-free version stayed around 3x slower, on another the gap shrank toward 2x as threads increased, and on a third it actually beat the lock-free queue once the thread count approached the core count. Most of the optimized version's gain came from helping at most one other thread per operation, chosen in cyclic order.

Their follow-up (PPoPP 2012) names the root cause: the **helping mechanism**. Typical wait-free algorithms help immediately on entry, interfering with operations that would have finished alone, and all threads help in the same order, duplicating each other's work and adding expensive CAS operations even at low contention. The fix is the **fast-path-slow-path** methodology.

scenes.caption: Before its own work, a thread checks its helping record: is the thread it last noted still stuck on the same slow-path phase? Usually not, so it skips straight to the fast path.
The fast path is a customized lock-free algorithm (here the Michael-Scott queue). Low contention: it succeeds on the first try and returns, with no announcing and no helping.
High contention: after MAX_FAILURES failed tries, the thread switches to the slow path, a customized Kogan-Petrank queue. It publishes its operation with a phase and keeps trying until done.

The slow path is bounded because other threads eventually help it: each checks its helping record once every HELPING_DELAY operations and moves to the next thread in cyclic order, so helpers spread out.

blocks.md: Two properties make the helping cheap. It is **delayed**: a thread notes a contending operation and checks only on a later operation whether it still needs help, in the hope that it finished by itself. It is **parallel**: each thread's helping record points to a different thread, advancing modulo the thread count, so helpers do not all pile onto the same operation. In the paper's evaluation the resulting queue performed like the Michael-Scott queue and substantially better than the original Kogan-Petrank queue, while keeping a bound on each operation's steps.

blocks.title: The same idea in a fetch-and-add queue (wfqueue.c)

scenes.caption: Yang and Mellor-Crummey's queue first publishes a hazard pointer for the segment it will touch, so a concurrent reclaimer cannot free it.
Patience defaults to MAX_PATIENCE = 10 in the source.

Fast path: enq_fast claims a cell index with one fetch-and-add on the enqueue counter, then CASes the cell's value from empty to v. It fails if the cell is no longer empty, for example because a dequeuer got there first and marked it unusable.
Each failure costs one unit of patience. The loop condition calls enq_fast before testing p, so a thread makes at most 11 fast attempts: the first plus 10 retries.
p is now below zero, so the thread publishes its request and takes the slow path, where dequeuers that reach its cells help complete it.
Done: the hazard pointer is released. In the common case the first enq_fast succeeds and the slow path never runs.

blocks.md: Memory reclamation must not quietly weaken the guarantee. A garbage collector is a dependency: Kogan and Petrank note that no wait-free GC was known when they wrote. Michael's **hazard pointers** are described in his paper as wait-free and applicable to wait-free algorithms without weakening their progress guarantee: a thread publishes the pointers it is about to dereference in single-writer slots, and a retired node is freed only when no slot holds it. One caution: the *protect* step (publish, then re-read the source to validate) can retry, so the surrounding algorithm must bound those retries too.

When is plain lock-free good enough? Alistarh, Censor-Hillel and Shavit analyze a broad class of lock-free algorithms (a preamble of $q$ steps, then a scan-and-validate loop of $s$ steps) under a uniform stochastic scheduler. There, such algorithms are wait-free with probability 1. Counting system steps (steps by all threads), the expected system latency is $O(q + s\sqrt{n})$ and each process's expected latency is exactly $n$ times that, so a thread's own expected steps per operation match the system latency. Lesson 1's simulation fits: a thread's own steps per increment (2 x the mean attempts, a load and a CAS each) went 2.86, 3.99, 5.53, 7.66 for 2 to 16 threads, close to $2\sqrt{n}$, with no hard ceiling on any one operation.

Choose wait-free when you need a **per-operation** bound: real-time threads, operations with a deadline or SLA, or heterogeneous systems where fast threads could keep starving slow ones. Otherwise lock-free usually suffices on real schedulers. Fast-path-slow-path lets you have both, and its authors note it can even give real-time threads a predictable maximum response time while other threads use only the fast path.

Check every layer. A wait-free algorithm is only as wait-free as its primitives and helpers: a `fetch_or` that compiles to a CAS loop, an allocator that takes a lock, or a reclamation scheme that can block will each reintroduce unbounded waiting.

blocks.question: In a fast-path-slow-path queue, the fast path is only lock-free. Why is each operation still wait-free?
options: Because the fast path almost always succeeds in practice
Because the fast path is tried at most MAX_FAILURES times, and the slow path completes in a bounded number of steps thanks to helping
Because fast and slow paths cannot run at the same time
Because MAX_FAILURES is set to the number of threads
blocks.explain: Wait-freedom is a worst-case property. The bound comes from capping the fast-path attempts and then relying on the wait-free slow path, whose bound comes from helping. It does not depend on the fast path usually succeeding, and the paper explicitly lets both paths run in parallel.

blocks.question: You port a wait-free queue from Java to C++ for a hard real-time control thread. Which reclamation choice keeps operations wait-free?
options: Free nodes through a global mutex-protected free list
Hazard pointers, as Kogan and Petrank propose
Never free nodes, but allocate each one with a malloc that may take a lock
Defer frees until all threads pass a quiescent point, waiting if one is delayed
blocks.explain: A mutex, a locking allocator, or waiting for every thread to reach a quiescent point all let one delayed thread stall others. Michael describes hazard pointers as wait-free and usable inside wait-free algorithms without weakening their guarantee, which is why the paper suggests them.

blocks.question: With MAX_PATIENCE = 10, at most how many times does wfqueue's `enqueue` call `enq_fast` before switching to the slow path?
options: Unbounded
blocks.explain: The loop calls enq_fast first and only then tests and decrements p. Calls 1 to 10 fail with p at 10 down to 1, each passing the test; call 11 fails with p at 0, the test fails and p drops to -1. So 11 fast attempts, then enq_slow.
